title: Addis Ababa Messages from the 17th Internet Governance Forum (2022) on Global Digital Compact Themes
executive_summary: The 17th Internet Governance Forum (IGF) in Addis Ababa (2022) focused on five key themes aligned with the UN's proposed Global Digital Compact (GDC): connecting all people while safeguarding human rights; avoiding Internet fragmentation; governing data and protecting privacy; enabling safety, security, and accountability; and addressing advanced technologies including AI. Discussions emphasized closing digital divides, especially for marginalized groups and women, ensuring meaningful access beyond connectivity, and embedding human rights in digital development. The forum highlighted the risks of Internet fragmentation due to technical, commercial, and policy factors, advocating for multistakeholder governance and international cooperation. Data governance calls for coherent global frameworks balancing privacy, justice, and cross-border flows. Cybersecurity and cybercrime require coordinated, rights-respecting policies, with attention to misinformation and digital literacy. Advanced technologies like AI must be human-centered, transparent, and inclusive, with global standards developed through multistakeholder engagement to uphold rights and foster trust.
characteristics: The 17th Internet Governance Forum (IGF) focused on five key themes aligned with the UN's proposed Global Digital Compact: connectivity and human rights, avoiding internet fragmentation, data governance and privacy, safety and security, and advanced technologies including AI.

Emphasis on closing digital divides, especially for least developed countries, rural areas, and marginalized groups, with a focus on meaningful access beyond connectivity, including affordability, literacy, and local content.
Strong advocacy for human rights online, including freedom of expression, privacy, and protection from harassment, with calls to avoid internet shutdowns and improve digital rights monitoring.
Calls for multistakeholder governance to maintain an open, interoperable global internet and to address risks of fragmentation from technical, commercial, and policy factors.
Data governance highlighted as critical, with emphasis on privacy as a human right, the need for coherent global frameworks, data justice, and protection in AI and cross-border data flows.

Safety and security discussions stressed cybersecurity, cybercrime, misinformation, and accountability, alongside the environmental impact of digital technologies and the need for inclusive, rights-respecting AI governance.
practical_applications: IGF Dynamic Coalitions are actively addressing specific challenges related to the thematic areas of the Global Digital Compact and intend to contribute to its preparatory and implementation phases.

Governments and multistakeholder partners support the establishment and work of effective regulatory agencies and frameworks to improve connectivity, including innovative approaches such as community networks, appropriate spectrum allocation, and low earth orbit satellite access.
Community-led helplines and resources in local languages are being supported to help women resist and redress online gender-based violence.
Standards development organizations are encouraged to invite participation by experts in online human rights from all stakeholder communities.

Governments, private sector, and technical community are urged to avoid cybercrime laws and standards that negatively affect cybersecurity defenders and to facilitate multistakeholder engagement in policy development.
International initiatives have been established to support cybersecurity capacity-building integrated into broader digital development efforts.

The United Nations is encouraged to promote global adoption of key cybersecurity standards through the Global Digital Compact, advocacy, capacity building, and initiatives to test and monitor deployment.

Educational curricula are being encouraged to include digital literacy skills to empower citizens to identify disinformation and increase online safety awareness, with initiatives involving parents, teachers, and guardians.
Civil society participation in cybercrime and cybersecurity discussions is supported through education and resource gathering.
Independent oversight bodies with mandates to manage data registration, provide guidance, investigate, and resolve complaints from data subjects are recommended.
Multistakeholder input is promoted in the development of data governance policies to ensure understanding of implementation challenges.
Regional and global cooperation efforts are encouraged to enhance institutional capacities in developing economies for data governance.
Stakeholders from technical and non-technical communities are collaborating to develop flexible principles, guidelines, and standards to foster trust in AI systems.
Efforts are underway to improve translation accuracy and relevance of platform community standards and guidelines to enable better user understanding across different languages.
Support for professional journalism and media is recognized as part of efforts to address disinformation.
The IGF Policy Network on Internet Fragmentation is an active multistakeholder initiative addressing risks of Internet fragmentation.
Governments, private sector, and technical community are encouraged to coordinate and cooperate regionally and internationally to maintain Internet openness and interoperability.
Capacity-building policies for AI literacy, skills development, and language resources for minority languages are being promoted to support a global approach to advanced technologies.

kpi_list.kpi_text: The UN Secretary-General’s proposed Global Digital Compact (GDC) has as its first principle to “Connect all people to the Internet, including all schools.”
kpi_list.target_description: Connect all people to the Internet, including all schools
kpi_list.measurement_method: Assessment of global Internet connectivity rates and school connectivity coverage

kpi_list.kpi_text: Yet 2.7 billion people remain unconnected today, with those in least developed countries and rural communities most disadvantaged.
kpi_list.target_description: Reduce the number of unconnected people from 2.7 billion to zero

kpi_list.kpi_text: SDG target 9c, which seeks to achieve universal, affordable Internet access, cannot be met until this gap is closed [gender digital gap].
kpi_list.target_description: Close the gender digital gap to achieve universal, affordable Internet access
kpi_list.measurement_method: Monitoring gender-disaggregated Internet access and usage data

kpi_list.kpi_text: Governments should protect and promote required infrastructure, including grid and off-grid power as well as communications networks.
kpi_list.target_description: Ensure resilient and secure digital infrastructure including power and communications networks
kpi_list.measurement_method: Infrastructure resilience assessments and regulatory frameworks in place

kpi_list.kpi_text: The United Nations could help accelerate the global adoption of key standards by including their promotion in the Global Digital Compact, by supporting advocacy and capacity building and by encouraging initiatives to test and monitor deployment.
kpi_list.target_description: Accelerate global adoption and deployment of cybersecurity standards
kpi_list.timeframe: by 2024 (Summit of the Future) and ongoing
kpi_list.measurement_method: Tracking adoption rates and implementation of cybersecurity standards globally
kpi_list.responsible_entity: United Nations, Governments, Private Sector, Technical Community

kpi_list.kpi_text: Developing economies need to enhance their institutional capacities to govern, use and manage data in a comprehensive, objective and evidence-based manner, including through regional and global cooperation.
kpi_list.target_description: Enhance institutional capacities in developing economies for effective data governance
kpi_list.measurement_method: Capacity assessments and evidence of regional/global cooperation initiatives
kpi_list.responsible_entity: Developing Country Governments, Regional Bodies, International Organizations

kpi_list.kpi_text: Capacity-building is important in efforts to address advanced technologies. Policies for AI literacy, skills development and language resources for minority languages are needed in order to formulate a truly global approach to advanced technologies.
kpi_list.target_description: Develop policies and programs for AI literacy, skills development, and minority language resources
kpi_list.measurement_method: Existence and implementation of AI literacy and skills programs; availability of language resources

kpi_list.kpi_text: Governments and regulators should ensure that personal data are protected, identifying the differentiated responsibilities of different stakeholders and without imposing undue burdens or responsibilities on individual users.
kpi_list.target_description: Ensure effective personal data protection with clear stakeholder responsibilities and enforcement mechanisms
kpi_list.measurement_method: Existence and enforcement of data protection laws and oversight bodies

kpi_list.kpi_text: Educational curricula should include digital literacy skills that help children to be safe online. Initiatives should involve parents, teachers and guardians.
kpi_list.metric_name: Digital Literacy Education for Online Safety
kpi_list.target_description: Integrate digital literacy and online safety skills into educational curricula with stakeholder involvement
kpi_list.measurement_method: Curriculum reviews and implementation reports; stakeholder engagement records

sdg_alignment: SDG 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth
SDG 16: Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions

top_actors.name: Governments
top_actors.justification: Governments are frequently mentioned as key actors responsible for infrastructure, regulatory frameworks, cybersecurity, data governance, and international cooperation. They play a central role in implementing policies, protecting human rights online, and participating in multistakeholder governance and international agreements.

top_actors.name: United Nations
top_actors.justification: The United Nations is the overarching institutional framework within which the Internet Governance Forum operates. It hosts the IGF, proposes the Global Digital Compact, and is involved in setting global agendas, norms, and standards related to Internet governance, human rights, and digital development.

top_actors.name: Civil Society Organisations
top_actors.justification: Civil society organisations are highlighted as important stakeholders in multistakeholder governance, policy development, capacity building, and advocacy. They contribute to discussions on human rights, digital inclusion, cybersecurity, and content moderation, ensuring diverse voices and expertise are included.

top_themes.name: Digital Inclusion
top_themes.justification: Digital Inclusion is a central theme throughout the document, emphasized in the first major section and underpinning the Global Digital Compact's first principle to connect all people. The extensive discussion on digital divides, gender digital gaps, infrastructure, and meaningful access highlights its strategic importance for equitable development and human rights realization.

top_themes.name: Data Governance
top_themes.justification: Data Governance is a major focus, with a dedicated section addressing the complexity of data flows, privacy, justice, cross-border issues, and the need for coherent global frameworks. It is strategically critical given data's role as a key resource in the digital economy and its direct impact on trust, security, and human rights.

top_themes.name: Cybersecurity
top_themes.justification: Cybersecurity is extensively covered, addressing threats, policy challenges, capacity building, and the need for multistakeholder cooperation. It is vital for ensuring a safe and resilient Internet, which is foundational to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and maintaining trust in digital technologies.
